extracted.intended_audience: empirical economists, policy researchers, and applied econometricians studying mortgage markets, shadow banking, and fintech
extracted.subtask_short: empirical robustness checks for mortgage lending
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical-implementation standards used in an applied study of fintech and shadow-bank mortgage lending, including classification rules, sample-selection sensitivity tests, counterfactual decomposition methods, and econometric robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual decomposition of drivers (regulation vs technology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a calibrated model to infer how much of shadow-banking and fintech growth is attributable to increased regulatory burden versus technological improvements by setting key parameters to baseline (2008) values and letting other fitted parameters evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct counterfactuals by (a) fixing bank regulatory burden and fintech quality to 2008 levels (baseline) and report growth of non-fintech and fintech shadow banks; (b) fix fintech quality to 2008 but allow regulatory burden to evolve (to quantify regulatory effects); (c) fix regulatory burden to 2008 but allow fintech quality to evolve (to quantify technological effects). Report percentages attributable to each channel and residual unexplained growth. Example outcomes: regulation-only accounts for ~60% of shadow-bank growth; technology-only accounts for ~30% of shadow-bank growth and ~90% of fintech gains in market share (paper's calibrated numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lender classification: multiple independent coders and conservative tie-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify lenders (bank vs nonbank; fintech vs non-fintech) using multiple independent research assistants (RAs) to cross-validate judgments and resolve disagreements conservatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When RAs disagree, adopt the conservative choice (the authors classify disputed lenders as non-fintech). Report that RAs together with authors arrive at substantively similar classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical verification of classification using archived websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that lender classifications (fintech vs non-fintech) at the time of analysis are appropriate at the start of the sample period by examining archived versions of lenders' websites (e.g., Internet Archive Wayback Machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the largest lenders, check that those classified as fintech in 2016 would have been fintech in 2008-2010 and non-fintech lenders would have been non-fintech. Note limits: archived pages are inactive and may not allow verification of the full online application or firm-offer processes; use additional restrictions (e.g., restrict fintech classification to large participants known to offer firm-offer rates throughout the sample) if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-selection robustness: run multiple restricted samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Rerun main analyses on alternative samples to assess sensitivity to sample construction choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended robustness samples include: (1) restrict HMDA to the top 50 lenders (to improve comparability with GSE data), (2) restrict Fannie/Freddie data to retail originations only, (3) exclude a dominant outlier (e.g., Quicken Loans) to test influence of largest firms, and (4) limit the time window (e.g., 2010-2013) to see if recent technology improvements drive results. Report whether qualitative results hold and discuss power loss when excluding major players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier/influential-firm checks (exclude large firms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether key findings are driven by one or a few very large firms by reestimating results excluding the largest market participant(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When excluding a dominant firm (Quicken Loans example), note decreased statistical power and carefully document which substantive results persist (e.g., fintech specialization in refinances; faster sale of originated loans; higher interest rates; interest rates less-explained by observables) and which change (e.g., relative rate differences shrink).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check alternative explanations for observed price differences (origination fees/points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether observed higher interest rates for a lender group are compensated by lower origination fees or points when comprehensive fee data are not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct manual checks (e.g., reviews, firm-level information) and report findings. In the paper, manual investigation and online reviews suggested fintech (Quicken) charged high origination fees rather than compensating borrowers with lower fees; reference an appendix for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative datasets and report data limitations/caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Test robustness of interest-rate and other findings using other datasets (e.g., FHA data), while explicitly acknowledging missing variables that limit inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using FHA data, note the lack of borrower credit-score information and the potential for uncontrolled selection; interpret differences cautiously and report consistency or divergence from conforming-loan analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Econometric specification robustness: controls and fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate specifications with and without borrower and loan controls and with different fixed-effect structures to assess robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare models with quarter fixed effects only to models with zip-quarter (or zip x quarter) fixed effects and with borrower and loan covariates. Present both sparse and fully controlled specifications; report how coefficients change across them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-error clustering robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess robustness of statistical significance to alternative clustering choices for standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary clustering: by geographical area cross time (e.g., zip-quarter or county-year). Robustness: cluster by lender × time to account for within-lender shocks. Report that main results' significance is unaffected by these alternative clustering choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent table and regression reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize tables and regression output to clearly describe samples, columns, fixed effects, controls, and base categories and to facilitate interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: label panels (A/B), report which columns include borrower/loan controls or fixed effects; explicitly state omitted/base categories for dummies (e.g., race omitted = White; sex omitted = Male; loan purpose omitted = Purchase; purchaser omitted = Not sold; loan type omitted = Conventional). Report sample sizes (N), R2, t-statistics in parentheses, and conventional significance stars (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-event measurement and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing time until sale (or similar time-to-event outcomes), define the left-hand-side variable and present mean values and interpretation in familiar units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: measure quarters between origination and sale; report mean in quarters and convert to days (e.g., 0.46 quarters ≈ 41 days). Use quarter fixed effects and include borrower/loan controls in alternate specifications. Cluster standard errors at an appropriate level (e.g., zip-quarter) and report t-statistics and significance.
